value: ClinicMind is an all-in-one healthcare SaaS platform that helps practices improve patient retention, reduce provider burnout, and manage revenue across the full care lifecycle. As the company began investing in UX maturity, I joined as the second designer to lead redesign across five core products — for both clinical and administrative users.

With a 20-year legacy, every product decision had been made by engineers. Design was a newborn function. On day one I faced not a design problem but a trust deficit: no authority, no inherited collaboration process, and no language to prove design was useful.
I knew that opening Figma and restyling buttons would only brand me "the person who makes things pretty."

blocks.value: Before pushing any design, I had to earn the right to be heard.

blocks.label: ClinicMind's platform — a 20-year, all-in-one healthcare SaaS

indexedSections.title: Four moves to earn the room

blocks.title: Make the team see a problem they'd stopped noticing

value: The first hard battle: engineers couldn't feel the problem. The system was complex and the flows convoluted — but after 20 years, that was just "how it is." You can't push a problem people can't see.

So I didn't argue about design. I ran discovery calls with our core users — physicians — even though their time is scarce and hard to get. I surfaced one fact with real impact: our doctors spend a huge share of their day not on patient care, but on note-taking, scheduling, and fighting with insurance companies.
I brought that back untouched. I didn't say "your design is bad." I said:

blocks.value: Our physicians spend half their day away from patients.
blocks.attribution: How I reframed the problem to the team

blocks.value: That turned an abstract "UX issue" into a human and business problem the team couldn't ignore — and for the first time, engineering saw it. That's the translation work: turning the doctor's language into language engineers act on.

blocks.label: Where a physician's day actually goes — discovery-call synthesis

blocks.title: Sell "slow down to speed up" to a team hungry to ship

value: Next I pushed a harder sell: stop piling on features — build a design system first.

Deeply counter-intuitive at the time: the team wanted output, and I was asking to invest in a foundation with no short-term deliverable — in a clinical, regulated domain where I had to learn the vocabulary as I went. My argument wasn't "it'll look better." It was ROI math: with one or two designers against 7+ engineers, negotiating every page from scratch means we never catch up; with an Atomic Design component library and clear documentation, every feature becomes assembly, and engineering has something concrete to build against.

blocks.value: Slow down once, so everyone moves faster afterward. Framed as ROI — not taste — the product owner bought in.

blocks.label: Atomic Design — the methodology behind the Vericle Design System
Effects and radii — specified on real dialog components
Spacing specs applied to real EHR components — Encounters and Vitals

value: What actually accelerated collaboration was changing how the team communicated. With no prototypes or specs, everything lived in words — and everyone pictured something different, so reviews spun in misunderstanding. So I did two high-leverage things:

items.label: Artifacts over words
items.title: Prototypes replace description
items.desc: Sketches and interactive prototypes gave every review one shared artifact to argue over — instead of five imagined versions.

items.label: Produce once, reuse endlessly
items.title: 30+ recorded demos
items.desc: Every page and interaction walked through on video, paired with Figma specs — always available to dev and business teams.

blocks.value: The demos let stakeholders see upcoming features early, turning them from passive recipients of a surprise change into co-builders. Alignment shifted from repeated debate to everyone aligning against the same visible truth.

blocks.label: Interactive prototypes — the thing everyone points at
One of the 30+ recorded demo walkthroughs

blocks.title: The finish line is a 1:1 build, not an approved mock

value: My definition of "driving design" was never "the mock got approved" — it was "the design shipped exactly as intended."

Previously, engineers implemented from their own interpretation, and the result drifted far from the design. Now, with the design system as a shared language and 30+ demos plus Figma specs as precise handoff, engineering could finally match my intent down to the interactions.

blocks.value: Communication stopped being a one-off handoff and became a continuously closing loop.

blocks.label: Design vs. built — side by side, 1:1

blocks.label: The redesigned appointment dashboard — cleaner and more organized

blocks.value: The real result wasn't how well I designed — it was that I made communication itself a team capability.

indexedSections.title: Let everyone see the same truth

value: In a place with no design culture, a designer's biggest output isn't mockups — it's getting the whole team to start thinking in terms of design. Not through authority, but by letting everyone see the same truth.

blocks.value: Advocating for design quality across teams starts before you have any formal power — and building that influence from the ground up is where I'm at my best.
